analysis.one_liner: Sets deadlines for the EPA to write federal limits on PFAS "forever chemicals" discharged into water by major industries.
analysis.headline: The bill has been referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its water subcommittee, with no further action since February 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are "forever chemicals" used in manufacturing that don't break down and are linked to serious health problems; they end up in rivers, lakes, and drinking water. This bill orders the EPA to set federal limits on how much PFAS major industries — chemical and plastics plants, metal finishers, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, and others — can discharge into water, with deadlines through 2028. It also starts immediate monitoring, locks in a standard test for detecting PFAS, and provides $200 million a year to help municipal wastewater plants screen out industrial PFAS before it reaches them.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water from rivers, lakes, and aquifers that receive industrial PFAS discharge — which is much of the country — gain lower exposure to chemicals linked to cancer, liver and thyroid problems, and developmental harm. Municipal water and wastewater utilities also benefit: the grants help them keep PFAS out of their systems, and upstream discharge limits reduce the cleanup burden they currently shoulder.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to set enforceable discharge limits (effluent limitations guidelines) for PFAS in nine industrial categories on a set schedule: organic chemicals and plastics, electroplating, and metal finishing by 2026; textile mills and landfills by 2027; leather tanning, paint, and plastics molding by 2028.

Requires the EPA to publish human health water quality criteria for every measurable PFAS within three years, giving states a scientific benchmark for cleaning up contaminated rivers, lakes, and drinking water sources.

Starts monitoring of PFAS discharges immediately upon enactment for the industries facing limits and for pulp and paper mills, airports, and electronics manufacturers, so regulators and the public can see who is releasing the chemicals.

Requires the EPA to officially adopt Method 1633A, the standard lab test for measuring PFAS in water, solid, and tissue samples, by January 31, 2026, so monitoring results are consistent and enforceable.

Authorizes $200 million per year through 2030 in grants to publicly owned wastewater treatment plants to intercept and treat industrial PFAS before it reaches them, and $12 million per year for the EPA's own work under the bill.

analysis.who_pays: The industries that discharge PFAS — chemical and plastics makers, electroplating and metal finishing shops, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, paint and plastics formulators, pulp and paper mills, airports, and electronics manufacturers — would pay for monitoring, testing, and treatment equipment to meet the new limits. Some costs could be passed to consumers. Federal taxpayers would fund the grants and EPA implementation if Congress appropriates the money.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes compliance and monitoring costs on a wide range of manufacturers, metal finishers, textile mills, landfills, and other dischargers, and some of those costs could be passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices.

The deadlines are ambitious for a regulatory agency: EPA must finalize rules for nine industry categories across three years and a water quality rule for every measurable PFAS, and federal rulemaking routinely takes longer than Congress expects, raising the risk of missed deadlines or litigation over rushed rules.

The $200 million annual grant program for wastewater treatment plants is authorized but 'subject to the availability of appropriations,' meaning Congress would still have to fund it each year for the pretreatment help to actually arrive.

Airports are covered by the monitoring requirement even though much airport PFAS comes from required firefighting foam, so the bill could impose testing costs on entities whose PFAS use is itself government-mandated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are potentially large and durable: enforceable limits on industrial PFAS discharges, with deadlines and a required test method, would reduce the "forever chemicals" entering drinking water sources, and $1 billion in grants would help wastewater plants stop industrial PFAS at the door [S2]. The costs are real but ordinary for pollution control: manufacturers, metal finishers, textile mills, and landfills would bear monitoring and treatment expenses that may be passed to consumers, airports would face testing costs tied to PFAS firefighting foam, and the ambitious rulemaking deadlines may be hard for EPA to meet, raising the risk of missed or weakened rules [S2]. On balance, the public-health upside outweighs the compliance costs, though the bill's dependence on annual appropriations could hollow out its grant program.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2025, referred to the House committee that handles water law, and then sent to that committee's water subcommittee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Chris Pappas introduced the bill on December 11, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican, signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor.
On February 2, 2026, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and no further action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial PFAS dischargers are better off for now, since no federal discharge limits have been set and nothing in the record requires them to change their behavior yet.

for.name: Rep. Chris Pappas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require PFAS discharge limits and water quality criteria, and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan from introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan but thin so far: one Democrat sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, with no recorded opposition or support beyond that.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers and industrial dischargers (organic chemicals, plastics, electroplating, metal finishing, textiles, tanning, paint)
industries.note: The bill would, for the first time, set enforceable federal limits on how much PFAS these plants may discharge into waterways and sewer systems, plus immediate monitoring. Compliance would require testing and often new treatment equipment. Today they can discharge PFAS with few federal limits, and the public absorbs the health and water-treatment cost.

Landfills face discharge limits by 2027 and airports face required monitoring, since landfill leachate and airport firefighting foam are significant PFAS sources. Their costs would rise, though the public's exposure to PFAS from these pathways would fall.

These municipal utilities receive $200 million a year in grants to monitor and pretreat industrial PFAS arriving at their plants. Currently they receive PFAS from industrial customers they cannot treat and can be held responsible for it; the grants and upstream discharge limits ease that burden.
Immediate monitoring requirements across the covered industries would create steady demand for PFAS analysis using the federally adopted Method 1633A test.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's water subcommittee, which is where most House bills stop. Similar PFAS-clean-water bills in recent Congresses died without a vote. Its chances depend on the subcommittee and full committee holding hearings and advancing it; with a single cosponsor so far, the realistic path to a floor vote this Congress is narrow, though it could be folded into a broader water resources or infrastructure package.
